claims.text: Pulse oximetry for severity; a blood gas if the child is in distress or tiring.
claims.quote: Severity is assessed by pulse oximetry and, in patients with respiratory distress or clinical signs of tiring, ABG measurement.

claims.text: Known asthma: bedside peak flow, or FEV1 when available.
claims.quote: Patients known to have asthma usually have bedside peak flow measurements (or, when available, forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1]).

claims.text: Chest X-ray for new or undiagnosed persistent wheezing; it can wait in a typical asthma flare.
claims.quote: Patients with new-onset or undiagnosed persistent wheezing should have a chest radiograph. Radiography can be deferred in patients with asthma who are having a typical exacerbation

claims.text: Sudden focal wheeze in a young child: inspiratory and expiratory chest X-rays; asymmetry suggests a foreign body.
claims.quote: In children, particularly preverbal children, who have sudden onset of focal wheezing, inspiratory and expiratory chest radiographs should be taken; asymmetric (or localized) findings suggest foreign body aspiration.

claims.text: Recurrent wheeze with an unclear diagnosis: pulmonary function testing; methacholine or exercise challenge if asthma is in question.
claims.quote: If the diagnosis is unclear in patients with recurrent wheezing, pulmonary function testing can confirm airflow limitation and quantify its reversibility and severity. Methacholine challenge testing and exercise testing can confirm airway hyperreactivity in patients for whom the diagnosis of asthma is in question.

claims.text: Bronchiolitis: pulse oximetry; a chest X-ray only with hypoxemia or severe distress.
claims.quote: Patients suspected of having bronchiolitis should undergo pulse oximetry to evaluate oxygenation. No further testing is required for mild cases with normal oxygen levels, but in cases of hypoxemia and severe respiratory distress, a chest radiograph supports the diagnosis
